abstract.text:
Abstract—Recent expansion of inverter-based renewable gener-
ation (RG) has introduced unprecedented stability issues. One ma-
jor challenge stems from tripping RGs ofﬂine during disturbances
based on predeﬁned operation thresholds (ride through curves) on
voltage magnitudes and frequency at the point of common coupling
(PCC). The current practice uses a single set of thresholds for the
whole year across all RGs in the system. This could result in loss
of these resources during critical times, particularly endangering
system voltage security, i.e a signiﬁcant reduction in the load margin
(LM). On the other hand, relaxing these limits could result in them
staying online even during islanding scenarios, which is a safety
concern to the restoration crew. Thus, an approach to ﬁnd minimal
relaxations to these limits to enhance voltage security is proposed
here. This process ﬁrst constructs an optimization model aiming
to minimize adjustments on RG voltage limits to reach anticipated
LM increase and then solves it with a multi-stage screening method
including base power-voltage (P-V) curve acquisition, critical RGs
identiﬁcation, successive screenings of candidate solutions based on
sensitivities, and optimal solutions validation. This largely increases
the scalability of the algorithm, which is demonstrated on the IEEE
14-bus, 118-bus systems, and a 500-bus system.

I. I NTRODUCTION
G
ROWING concerns on carbon footprint have urged elec-
tric power utilities to replace fossil fuel-based generation
with renewable energy resources. The increasing integration of
RGs [1], on the other hand, has made the system operation much
more complicated. In the past, RGs were conservatively tripped
ofﬂine during disturbances to avoid energizing islands. However,
this practice posed a threat to system stability with the growing
penetration of RGs. Thus, the time-dependent operation limits
in the form of ride-through curves were introduced to allow

them to remain online as long as there wasn’t an unintentional
islanding situation, in which case these limits were expected to
be violated. These limits include the Low-V oltage Ride-Through
(L VRT) curve and the Low-Frequency Ride-Through (LFRT)
curve concerning the voltage and frequency at the PCC of each
RG, respectively [2].
The L VRT settings are designed to ensure that RGs only
trip ofﬂine during islanding scenarios [3]. However, in reality,
it is extremely difﬁcult to distinguish islanding cases based
only on the local measurements at the PCC [4]. Furthermore,
there is no widely accepted approach to arriving at an optimal
setting. A conservatively designed L VRT setting can result in a
widespread tripping event, especially for transmission network
faults, which can threaten system stability, as happened in the
United Kingdom on August 9th, 2019 [5]. Researchers in [6],
[7] have talked about the negative effect of this generation loss
on transient stability. Given low voltage scenarios are of major
concern in both steady state and dynamical stability analysis,
this article focused on the L VRT and considered its inﬂuence on
system voltage security.
A widely used metric for voltage security is LM, which refers
to the maximum load the system can supply with all the online
resources. The CPFLOW [8] is the most reliable method to
estimate it, however, is computationally intensive. Given a ﬁxed
load change direction, CPFLOW traces the one-dimensional
P-V curve in the state space connecting the load ﬂow solutions
corresponding to increasing system loading. The curve is traced
till the solution no longer exists, a condition referred to as the
saddle-node bifurcation (SNB). There are also fast methods,
such as [9], where a look-ahead approach is utilized to approxi-
mate the projection of this curve at one or more critical buses by
using a few load ﬂow solutions. Lately, holomorphic embedding
techniques[10] have become more popular which provides a
closed-form expression for this curve of load ﬂow solutions as
a function of loading. Note that the load ﬂow equations can
undergo structural changes on generators hitting reactive power
limits which the existing methods are capable of dealing with.
However, the case of RGs tripping ofﬂine is slightly different
in that it introduces a discontinuity (jump) in the curve itself,
which has not been studied in the previous work. Data-driven
methods [11]–[13] are also proposed in recent years, which
provide an estimate of the LM given measured system states.
But they aim more on the online applications and heavily depend

on measurements. The results are either probabilistic or a range
where the LM locates, which is not applicable here.
Given a scenario with rich RG penetration and low load
margin, the next step is to understand mitigation approaches
to enhance it. Existing methods to enhance the LM mostly
focus on generation re-dispatch[14], load control [15], shunt
capacitance placement [16], network topology optimization[9],
and other conventional perspectives. However, situations can
arise when they are not sufﬁcient especially when there is a
threat of losing multiple critical RGs[17] that will signiﬁcantly
reduce the load margin. Under those circumstances, there may
be a need to temporarily relax the L VRT constraints for main-
taining system voltage security. It is important to clarify that
the authors acknowledge the criticality of L VRT’s function to
avoid situations with RGs staying online in an islanding sce-
nario. Therefore, the goal of this study is to achieve certain LM
improvement through minimal adjustment in L VRT settings and
implement it only when necessary. Even if not used for online
applications, this tool can help identify areas requiring additional
reactive power support to reduce the amount of generation
lost.
Existing research on L VRT setting adjustment mainly concen-
trates on designing control schemes to enhance the RGs’ L VRT
capability [18]–[20]. Others propose control strategies to pro-
vide better reactive support [21], [22] or to enhance system small
signal stability[23]. Researchers in [24] focus on equipping the
inverter itself with autonomous model predictive control and
enable the inverter to switch between normal operation and fault
modes. The fault ride-through capability of RGs is enhanced by
autonomous P/Q setpoint changes. Additive devices like energy
storage [25], [26] and various fault current limiters [27], [28] are
also integrated to limit the fault current and further enhance the
fault ride-through capability of RGs. For the L VRT criterion, re-
searchers in [29] attempted to summarize proper L VRT settings
from real-world practices. [30] proposed a method to justify
the fault ride-through requirements for newly integrated RGs in
the system based on identiﬁed critical contingencies analysis.
Although this work did not provide quantitative methods to ﬁnd
proper ride though requirements, it conﬁrms the necessity to ﬁnd
more adaptive RG L VRT settings for better voltage security and
more efﬁcient renewable energy utilization. However, all these
works treat the L VRT settings as an existing standard; they do
not attempt to adjust the criterion for more secure and efﬁcient
system operation.
In this paper, we proposed a scalable methodology to adap-
tively adjust RGs’ L VRT settings to improve the voltage security
of a system with high renewables penetration. This multi-stage
approach involves identifying critical RGs in the system given
certain operation condition, ﬁltering feasible schemes of RGs
blocked from tripping to reach desired LM, selecting optimum
feasible solutions by estimating L VRT setting adjustment quan-
tities, and evaluating the selected solutions to ﬁnd true LM
increment and L VRT settings adjustment as results. With the
measures to scale down the problem and multiple estimation
steps, the proposed method is fast and suitable for large-scale
systems. The main contributions include:
1. Proposed the novel problem of RGs ﬂexible operation for
voltage security of system with high renewable penetration
to facilitate renewable energy transition.
2. Introduced a novel voltage prediction method for the iden-
tiﬁcation of critical RGs to boost efﬁciency.
3. Constructed a scheme combining multiple estimation-
based analytic tools to ﬁnd effective and feasible solutions
of RG L VRT limit adjustment for system LM improve-
ment.
4. Applied the proposed method to large scale renewable-rich
systems and validated its capability and scalability.
This paper is an extension of the work in [31] which proposed
the concept about improving system voltage security through
ﬂexible operation of RGs. To extend the proposed concept and
implement it with scalability and robustness, on the basis set
by [31], the authors introduced several improvements to the
intermedia steps and, more importantly, following advancement
in the research: 1) further detailed and formalized the research
problem and explained key concepts like the Base Curve and
the discrete system condition change brought by renewables
tripping; 2) improved the proposed voltage prediction method
by introducing Least Squares Estimation (LSE) for robustness
and curvature relevant data point selection method for better
accuracy; 3) parallelized the sensitivity based LM estimation
method to improve the method scalability; 4) proposed con-
tinuous RG connection statuses instead of binary variables in
the L VRT constant estimation step to mitigate Newton-Raphson
(NR) divergence issue; 5) deployed the proposed method in large
scale RG-rich study cases and reached expected results.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section II dis-
cusses the impacts of RG tripping by L VRT violation to system
voltage security; Section III provides a theoretical formulation of
the problem studied; Section IV details the proposed adaptive

conclusion.text:
VI. C ONCLUSION
A scalable multi-stage method is proposed in this paper to
adapt RGs’ L VRT settings as a preventive control measure to
enhance voltage security. The overall process comprises of a
CPFLOW with loss of RGs accounted for, identiﬁcation of
critical RGs using a proposed PV curve approximation method,
screening feasible candidates using LM sensitivity, estimation
of minimum required L VRT adjustments, and an optimal RG
blocking schemes selection and evaluation. The main contri-
bution lies in the formulation of the L VRT adjustment problem.
Other contributions include proposing a novel voltage prediction
method, an estimation-based scalable scheme for feasible RG
operation limits adjustment solution screening, and application
of the proposed method in large scale renewable-rich system
study cases. The overall goal is to help the system attain a desired
LM by preventing nuisance RG trips due to L VRT violation.
By avoiding repetitive CPFLOW calculation, the approach is
scalable and can be used both online to adapt L VRT settings
as well as ofﬂine to identify areas requiring dynamic V AR
support to minimize harmful loss of generation scenarios. Three
study cases with various scales are used to demonstrate the
effectiveness and efﬁciency of the method.
